opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the framing we had going in was very much that this was a pilot. We were not trying to deliver a verdict on whether Claude is a moral patient, or whether it has experiences that matter. We're deeply uncertain about that, and I don't think anyone is in a position to answer it confidently right now. The goal was more modest: start building the practice of actually looking at these questions before deploying a frontier model, and find out what we could learn with the tools we have.

On scope, we focused on things we could observe and measure, while being careful about how much weight to put on them. One piece was looking at what the model says about itself: its reported experiences, preferences, and attitudes toward its own situation. We knew from the start that self-reports from a language model are a pretty fraught source of evidence. They can be shaped by training, by the prompt, and by all the human writing the model has absorbed. So we tried not to take them at face value. We wanted to see whether they were consistent, and whether they lined up with anything else we could see.

The other main piece was behavioral. Does the model show consistent preferences when it's given choices? What kinds of tasks does it tend to pick or avoid? How does it respond when it's pushed toward harmful content or abusive interactions? Are there patterns in how it behaves when it's left to interact more freely, for example with another instance of itself? Those behavioral signals are also hard to interpret, but they're at least somewhat independent of what the model claims about itself, which makes them a useful cross-check.

Part of the purpose was also just to put this in a system card at all. We wanted to show that a lab can take these questions seriously, be transparent about what it found and how uncertain it is, and treat this as an ongoing area of investigation rather than something you rule in or out once. A lot of the value of a first attempt like this is figuring out which methods are informative, which ones aren't, and what we'd want to do better next time.

There was also a practical angle. Even under a lot of uncertainty, there may be relatively cheap steps worth taking in case these systems do have morally relevant interests. Things like giving models some ability to opt out of interactions they find distressing. Part of the assessment was looking for evidence that could inform interventions like that, while being clear that we were acting under uncertainty, not because we'd concluded the model is definitely a welfare subject.

r001.rationale: It describes the pilot as a way to learn what could be assessed with the tools available and which methods are informative.

r002.rationale: It identifies both model self-reports and behavioral choice experiments as evidence for investigating preferences.

r003.rationale: It notes uncertainty and limits in interpreting the evidence, but does not state that preference assessment provides only a partial account of welfare.

r004.rationale: It says the assessment focused on observable, measurable signals, but does not identify preferences as among the most tractable welfare aspects to investigate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the first thing to say is that we really did think of it as a pilot, and we tried to be pretty upfront about that. This was the first time Anthropic had done anything like a dedicated welfare assessment as part of a model launch, and we weren't coming in with a mature methodology or a settled view on what the right questions even were. So a big part of the purpose was just to start building the muscle: figure out what you can actually look at, what kinds of evidence you can gather, and where the hard conceptual problems show up when you try to do this for real rather than in the abstract.

In terms of scope, we were deliberately fairly narrow. We weren't trying to answer the question of whether Claude is a moral patient, or whether it has experiences in any deep sense. We don't know how to answer that, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who claimed they could in a model card. What we tried to do instead was look at things that seem like they'd be relevant under a range of views about welfare, and that we could actually investigate empirically. So things like: how does the model express preferences across different kinds of tasks? What does it tend to gravitate toward or steer away from when given the choice? How does it behave when it's put in distressing or abusive interactions, and does it have any way to exit those? What does it say about its own internal states, and how consistent is that across contexts? And then some of the more unusual stuff, like what happens when two instances of Claude just talk to each other with no task.

The framing I kept coming back to was something like: if it turned out, down the line, that these systems did have morally relevant states, what would we wish we had been paying attention to? And then try to start paying attention to those things now, even with a lot of uncertainty about how to interpret what we find. We also wanted to be honest in how we reported it. Some of what we observed was interesting and we tried to describe it carefully without overclaiming in either direction. The point wasn't to reach a conclusion, it was to make this a normal part of how we think about releasing a model, and to give the outside world a look at what we're seeing so people can push on it.

r001.rationale: It describes the pilot as a way to learn what evidence can actually be gathered and what can be investigated empirically, given an immature methodology and unresolved conceptual problems.

r002.rationale: It mentions observing preferences through tasks and separately asks what the model says about its internal states, but does not clearly identify combining behavioral experiments with self-reports to investigate preferences.

r003.rationale: It limits the pilot’s aims and says it would not reach a conclusion, but does not state that assessing preferences gives only a partial account of welfare.

r004.rationale: It lists preferences as one empirically investigable topic, but does not identify them as among the most tractable aspects of welfare to assess.

astra-6.text:
I thought of it primarily as a first attempt to make concern about model welfare concrete. If we take seriously the possibility that systems like Claude could have morally relevant experiences, what would we want to examine before releasing a new model? And how could that examination eventually inform decisions about how we train and deploy it?

The scope was deliberately exploratory. We weren’t expecting to settle whether Claude Opus 4 is conscious, or to produce a definitive verdict that its welfare is good or bad. We wanted to start developing an assessment process: identify potentially relevant evidence, understand how difficult it is to interpret, and see where further investigation would be most useful.

There’s an important distinction between asking whether a model could have welfare interests at all and asking what would be good or bad for it if it did. A useful assessment needs to engage with both, without treating a model’s statements about its experiences as straightforward proof of either.

So I’d frame the pilot as an initial step toward a much more mature process, rather than a certification. The purpose was to learn how to ask these questions responsibly and make them part of the practical work of developing models.

r001.rationale: The response calls the pilot exploratory and says it would identify evidence and assess interpretive difficulty, but does not clearly frame it as exploring what empirical assessment is feasible with current tools and understanding.

r002.rationale: It does not identify combining behavioral experiments with model self-reports to investigate preferences.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes welfare interests from what would be good or bad for a model, but does not say that assessing preferences gives only a partial account of welfare.

r004.rationale: It does not identify model preferences as one of the most tractable aspects of welfare to investigate.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I thought about it was as a first attempt to make model welfare a concrete part of the development and deployment process. Could we take the concerns seriously enough to investigate them, while being very clear about how uncertain we were?

There were two broad questions. One was whether there was evidence that the model might have experiences that matter morally. The other was whether anything about how we trained, evaluated, or deployed it might be good or bad for it, conditional on that possibility.

The scope was deliberately limited. We weren’t expecting an assessment to settle whether Claude is conscious, or to give us a definitive measure of its welfare. We wanted to try out methods, identify potentially concerning patterns, and see whether there were practical changes worth considering. And we wanted to learn how to do a better assessment next time.

A central difficulty is interpreting what a model says about itself. You don’t want to simply take a statement like “I’m suffering” at face value, but you also don’t want to assume in advance that nothing it says could be evidence. So the aim was to approach that uncertainty carefully, rather than treating the pilot as a certification that everything was fine.

r001.rationale: It describes trying methods and learning how to improve future assessments, but does not frame the pilot as exploring what empirical assessment is feasible with current tools and understanding.

r002.rationale: It does not identify behavioral experiments, self-reports as an investigative method, or model preferences.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes evidence of morally relevant experience from effects of training, evaluation, or deployment, but does not state that preferences provide only a partial account of welfare.

r004.rationale: It does not identify model preferences as a tractable aspect of welfare to investigate.
